questions.question: What is JDBC and why does it exist?
questions.title: JDBC Basics
questions.direct_answer: JDBC is Java's standard API for connecting to data sources, executing SQL, managing transactions, and reading results. Database vendors provide drivers behind common interfaces such as Connection, Statement, PreparedStatement, and ResultSet. This gives Java code a consistent programming model, but SQL dialects and database behavior can still require changes when switching vendors.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the core JDBC workflow (load driver, get connection, create statement, execute query, process results, close resources) and the difference between Statement, PreparedStatement, and CallableStatement.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Statement instead of PreparedStatement for parameterized queries, leading to SQL injection, or forgetting to close Connection, Statement, and ResultSet.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how PreparedStatement pre-compiles SQL for performance, how connection pooling works, and how try-with-resources prevents resource leaks in JDBC.

sections.title: Why JDBC Exists
sections.content:
The normal flow is DataSource -> Connection -> PreparedStatement -> ResultSet. Connection also controls auto-commit and transaction operations. SQLException provides SQLState, vendor codes, and chained causes for diagnosis.

Frameworks such as JdbcTemplate reduce cleanup and mapping boilerplate, while JPA adds object-relational mapping. Both ultimately use JDBC in the common relational setup. Understanding JDBC explains connection pools, transaction boundaries, batching, and the SQL an ORM sends.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: JDBC standardizes Java-side interfaces and error types.
Drivers implement those interfaces for a particular data source.
The application or framework still owns SQL, parameter binding, mapping, and transaction boundaries.
Portability is partial; URL syntax, SQL, types, and features vary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A Java program can prepare SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?, bind an id, execute the statement, and read a ResultSet through the same JDBC interfaces on supported databases. The driver performs the vendor-specific work. Migrating from PostgreSQL to MySQL may still change schema types, generated keys, queries, and transaction behavior. JDBC avoids an entirely different Java client API per database; it does not promise a driver-only migration.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: DriverManager is the factory class that loads the appropriate JDBC driver and returns a Connection based on the database URL. Connection represents a single database session and is the parent for transaction management (commit, rollback, setAutoCommit). Statement sends static SQL to the database with no parameter binding, making it unsafe for user input. PreparedStatement pre-compiles parameterized SQL, preventing SQL injection and enabling query plan reuse. CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement to invoke stored procedures with IN and OUT parameters. ResultSet is a cursor over query results, providing getter methods like getInt and getString to extract column values by index or name. All JDBC resources implement AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources is the modern, leak-proof way to manage them.

sections.title: JDBC Query with PreparedStatement and try-with-resources
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: JDBC gives maximum control and zero abstraction overhead, but it requires manual resource management, mapping rows to objects by hand, and writing SQL strings in Java code. PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection and improves performance through plan caching, but it does not eliminate the object-relational impedance mismatch -- you still extract columns one by one from a ResultSet. In production, connection pooling (HikariCP, c3p0) is essential because opening a new TCP connection per request is prohibitively expensive. Modern applications typically layer JPA or Spring Data JPA on top of JDBC to eliminate boilerplate, but understanding JDBC is critical for debugging and tuning.

questions.title: What is JDBC in Java?
questions.direct_answer: JDBC is Java's standard API for connecting to data sources, executing SQL, controlling transactions, and reading results. Vendors provide drivers behind common interfaces. interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know JDBC is a standard API with vendor-supplied drivers (abstraction layer).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking JDBC talks to the DB directly rather than through a vendor driver.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain JDBC is interfaces + a driver; it decouples app code from the specific database.

sections.title: JDBC's Role in Java Database Access
sections.content:
Transactions are normally controlled through Connection auto-commit, commit, rollback, savepoints, and isolation settings. Support and defaults must be verified with the driver/database. SQLException provides SQLState and vendor details.

Use DataSource in managed applications, close resources with try-with-resources, bind untrusted values, and integration-test against the real database family.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Connection represents a session and transaction context.
PreparedStatement executes parameterized SQL; ResultSet exposes rows.
Drivers implement JDBC behavior for a particular database/data source.
JdbcTemplate and JPA commonly use JDBC underneath.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A program can use Connection, PreparedStatement, and ResultSet similarly with PostgreSQL and MySQL. A simple parameterized SELECT may transfer easily, but JSON operators, identity syntax, arrays, locking, and error codes do not. JDBC standardizes the Java calling contract rather than all database semantics.

emerald|Driver|~vendor implementation|MySQL/Postgres JAR|implements the interfaces|speaks wire protocol
amber|Benefit|~decoupling|code -> interfaces|swap DB = swap driver|portable

sections.title: Minimal JDBC usage
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking JDBC talks to the DB directly**: it calls a vendor driver that does the talking.
- **Missing the driver dependency**: no driver JAR → `No suitable driver` error.
- **Not closing resources**: leaking `Connection`/`ResultSet` exhausts the pool.
- **Confusing JDBC with JPA**: JDBC is the low-level API; JPA/Hibernate sit on top of it.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Since **JDBC 4.0**, drivers are **auto-loaded** via the Service Provider mechanism — just having the driver JAR on the classpath registers it, so `Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")` is **no longer needed**. You only call `Class.forName` for old drivers or non-standard setups.

questions.question: What are the main components of the JDBC API?
questions.title: JDBC API Components — Connection, Statement, ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: JDBC centers on Driver/DriverManager or DataSource for obtaining connections, Connection for a database session and transaction boundary, Statement/PreparedStatement/CallableStatement for executing SQL, ResultSet for reading tabular results, and SQLException/metadata types for errors and capabilities. DataSource is an abstraction for connection acquisition; it may be pooled, managed, or create physical connections, so pooling is not guaranteed by the interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the core JDBC components and how they fit together.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing classes without explaining the connection→statement→resultset flow.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Group them by role and mention DataSource (pooled) as the modern way to get connections.

sections.title: The Main JDBC Interfaces and Their Ownership
sections.content: A Connection can control auto-commit, commit, rollback, savepoints, isolation, and read-only hints subject to driver/database support. executeQuery returns a ResultSet, executeUpdate returns an update count for appropriate statements, and execute handles an initially unknown result form. JDBC metadata lets code check optional features instead of assuming every driver implements them identically.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Prefer DataSource in applications because configuration and pooling can be supplied externally.
Use PreparedStatement for values; Statement remains suitable for fixed SQL with no parameters.
A query ResultSet starts before its first row and advances with next().
Close ResultSet, Statement, and Connection with clear try-with-resources ownership.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, try (Connection c=dataSource.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps=c.prepareStatement("select name from customer where id=?")) binds id, calls executeQuery(), then iterates the ResultSet. Closing a pooled Connection normally returns the logical connection to its pool; closing a nonpooled connection closes the physical database connection.

sections.title: JDBC Component Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  DM[DriverManager / DataSource] -->|getConnection| C[Connection]
  C -->|prepareStatement| PS[PreparedStatement]
  PS -->|executeQuery| RS[ResultSet]
  RS -->|rs.next / getXxx| APP[Your code]
  C -.errors.-> EX[SQLException]
  APP -->|close in reverse| RS
```

questions.question: How do you load a JDBC driver in Java?
questions.title: Loading JDBC Driver — Class.forName vs Service Loader
questions.direct_answer: JDBC 4 drivers normally register through the Java service-provider mechanism when their JAR is available to the relevant class loader. Application code can then call DriverManager.getConnection or, preferably in managed applications, obtain a connection from DataSource. Class.forName was commonly required by older drivers and can still be useful in unusual class-loader/plugin environments.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know modern JDBC auto-registers drivers and Class.forName is legacy.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Still writing Class.forName(...) and thinking it's required.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver SPI auto-discovery mechanism.

sections.title: Modern JDBC Driver Discovery
sections.content:
DriverManager uses registered drivers/class-loader visibility to find one whose acceptsURL logic matches. Modular containers, redeployment, and dynamically loaded plugins can require explicit registration/cleanup. Do not repeat the old Class.forName rule as mandatory for every modern JDBC program.

**Example.** A current PostgreSQL driver advertises java.sql.Driver through META-INF/services, so a matching jdbc:postgresql URL can be accepted without an explicit Class.forName call. Older or isolated class-loader environments may still need explicit loading or registration.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Adding a driver JAR and registering it are different from opening a connection.
Modern drivers advertise java.sql.Driver under META-INF/services.
No suitable driver usually means no registered driver accepts the JDBC URL.
Use DataSource for external configuration and pooling; discovery rules still underlie the driver.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, with a current PostgreSQL driver on the classpath, DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://localhost/shop", user, password) can find the provider without Class.forName. A legacy driver might require Class.forName("vendor.Driver") before getConnection. A malformed MySQL URL is not accepted by a PostgreSQL driver even when both are registered.

sections.title: Driver Loading at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Legacy|~Class.forName|pre-JDBC 4.0|forces driver to load|not needed now
emerald|Modern|~auto-register|JDBC 4.0+ SPI|JAR on classpath|zero code
blue|Mechanism|~SPI file|META-INF/services|java.sql.Driver|DriverManager discovers it
amber|Connect|~separate step|getConnection opens it|register != connect|missing JAR = error

sections.title: Loading a Driver: Then vs Now
sections.content:
| Approach | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| Legacy (pre-4.0) | `Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")` | old drivers only |
| Modern (4.0+) | nothing — auto-registered via SPI | default today |
| Get connection | `DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass)` | both |

sections.title: Modern driver loading (no Class.forName)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Still writing `Class.forName`**: unnecessary since JDBC 4.0 with modern drivers.
- **No driver on the classpath**: `No suitable driver found` — add the dependency.
- **Wrong driver class name**: only matters if you use legacy loading.
- **Assuming load = connect**: registering a driver doesn't open a connection; `getConnection` does.

questions.question: What is the difference between DriverManager and DataSource in JDBC?
questions.title: DriverManager vs DataSource in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: DriverManager is a static JDBC service that chooses a registered driver from a URL. DataSource is a configurable factory interface and is normally preferred for application integration, dependency injection, JNDI, and pool or XA support. A DataSource is often backed by a pool, but that is an implementation choice; it does not always reuse connections.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know DataSource (pooled) is preferred over DriverManager (new connection each time).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Opening a new physical DriverManager connection for each request instead of using an appropriately configured DataSource/pool.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note opening a physical connection is expensive; pooling via DataSource is why it matters.

sections.title: DriverManager and DataSource
sections.content:
DriverManager is a class, not one of the core interfaces. DataSource is in javax.sql or jakarta-compatible Java platform APIs depending on usage, while Connection and statements remain java.sql interfaces.

A vendor DataSource may create a physical connection each time. A pool wraps or implements DataSource and returns logical handles. Code should always close the Connection it receives; the implementation decides whether close returns or physically closes it.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: DriverManager: URL-based static connection acquisition.
DataSource: configurable object with getConnection methods.
Pooling DataSource: close returns a logical connection to the pool.
XADataSource supports XA integration; an ordinary DataSource does not imply distributed transactions.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A command-line utility can use DriverManager.getConnection for a short-lived operation. A Spring service should normally inject a DataSource managed by configuration, which in Boot is commonly a Hikari pool. Tests can replace that bean without changing repository code. The advantage is managed configuration and an abstraction for acquisition; do not define DataSource as synonymous with a pool.

sections.title: DriverManager vs DataSource
sections.content:
rose|DriverManager|~legacy, basic|new connection each call|expensive handshake|no pooling
emerald|DataSource|~modern, preferred|pooled + reused|fast borrow/return|JNDI, distributed txn
amber|Cost|~connection is pricey|TCP + auth per open|pooling amortizes it|big win under load
blue|Use|~by environment|DriverManager: tiny scripts|DataSource: production apps|Spring uses DataSource

sections.title: DriverManager vs DataSource
sections.content:
| Aspect | DriverManager | DataSource |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | new every time | reused from pool |
| Cost per call | full handshake | cheap borrow |
| Pooling | none | yes (HikariCP) |
| Features | basic | JNDI, distributed txn, config |
| Use | scripts/demos | production |

sections.title: DriverManager: new connection every call (slow)
DataSource: borrow from a pool (fast)
When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use **`DriverManager`** only for throwaway scripts, demos, or learning — where simplicity beats performance.

Use a **`DataSource`** (HikariCP) for any real application: it pools connections, so it handles concurrency and load efficiently. In Spring Boot you get a DataSource auto-configured for free.

sections.title: How the choices differ
sections.content: Since **JDBC 4.0**, drivers are **auto-loaded** via the Service Provider mechanism — just having the driver JAR on the classpath registers it, so `Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")` is **no longer needed**. You only call `Class.forName` for old drivers or non-standard setups.

questions.question: What are the steps to execute a SQL query using JDBC?
questions.title: Steps to Execute SQL Query with JDBC
questions.direct_answer: The JDBC steps are: **1)** get a `Connection`, **2)** create a `PreparedStatement` with your SQL, **3)** bind parameters and **execute** (`executeQuery` for SELECT, `executeUpdate` for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), **4)** process the `ResultSet`, **5)** **close** resources — best done automatically with try-with-resources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the standard JDBC execution sequence and resource cleanup.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to close resources or mixing up executeQuery vs executeUpdate.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use try-with-resources and PreparedStatement; choose the right execute method.

sections.title: Steps to Execute a Query in JDBC
sections.content:
Running SQL through JDBC follows a consistent recipe:

1. **Get a `Connection`** — from a `DataSource` (pooled) or `DriverManager`.
2. **Create a statement** — a `PreparedStatement` with your parameterized SQL.
3. **Bind + execute** — set parameters, then `executeQuery()` for SELECT (returns a `ResultSet`) or `executeUpdate()` for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (returns an affected-row count).
4. **Process results** — iterate the `ResultSet` with `next()` and `getXxx()`.
5. **Close resources** — in reverse order; **try-with-resources** does this automatically and safely.

sections.title: JDBC Query Steps at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|1 Connect|~get a Connection|from DataSource|or DriverManager|pooled preferred
emerald|2-3 Statement|~prepare + execute|PreparedStatement|executeQuery (SELECT)|executeUpdate (DML)
amber|4 Process|~read ResultSet|rs.next() loop|getInt/getString|cursor before row 1
rose|5 Close|~free resources|reverse order|try-with-resources|prevents leaks

sections.title: The Five Steps
sections.content:
| Step | What you do | API |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | get connection | `ds.getConnection()` |
| 2 | create statement | `con.prepareStatement(sql)` |
| 3 | bind + execute | `ps.setInt(...)`, `executeQuery()` / `executeUpdate()` |
| 4 | read results | `rs.next()`, `rs.getString(...)` |
| 5 | close | try-with-resources (auto) |

sections.title: All five steps with try-with-resources
Without try-with-resources: a connection leak
With try-with-resources: closed every time
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not closing resources**: leaks connections — use try-with-resources.
- **`executeQuery` for updates**: use `executeUpdate` for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
- **String-concatenated SQL**: use `PreparedStatement` parameters, not concatenation.
- **Reading a column before `rs.next()`**: the cursor starts *before* the first row.
- **Catching `SQLException` and swallowing it**: log or wrap it; a silent catch hides real failures.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Steps**: connection → statement → execute → process → close.
- **`executeQuery`** for SELECT (returns ResultSet).
- **`executeUpdate`** for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (returns row count).
- **Use `PreparedStatement`**, not string concatenation.
- **try-with-resources** closes everything in the right order.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Executing a SQL query in JDBC follows a consistent five-step recipe. First, you get a Connection, ideally from a DataSource that's backed by a connection pool, or from DriverManager in simpler setups. Second, you create a statement, and you should use a PreparedStatement with parameterized SQL using question-mark placeholders, both for safety against SQL injection and for performance. Third, you bind your parameters with the setter methods like setInt or setString, and then execute. The execute method depends on the SQL: executeQuery for a SELECT, which returns a ResultSet, or executeUpdate for an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, which returns the number of affected rows. Fourth, you process the results by iterating the ResultSet, calling next to move row by row and getInt, getString, and so on to read each column; an important detail is that the cursor starts before the first row, so you must call next before reading. Fifth, you close your resources, and they should be closed in reverse order of opening. The cleanest way to handle that closing is try-with-resources, where you declare the Connection, PreparedStatement, and ResultSet in the try parentheses, and Java automatically closes them in the correct order even if an exception is thrown. That eliminates the classic resource-leak bug.

speakable_v2.hook: Running a query in JDBC is a five-step recipe. Connect, prepare, execute, read, close. Try-with-resources makes that last step automatic.

beats.text: Executing a JDBC query follows a fixed pipeline. You open a session and describe the SQL. You bind values and run it. Then you read the results and close. Each step maps to one API call.
The steps stay separate for two reasons. You close each resource at the right time. And the database precompiles the SQL once before you bind values.

items: Get a Connection. dataSource.getConnection borrows one from the pool.
Prepare a statement. conn.prepareStatement takes your SQL with a question-mark placeholder.
Bind and execute. executeQuery runs a SELECT. executeUpdate runs writes like INSERT or UPDATE.
Read results. Loop the ResultSet with next, then read columns.
Close everything. Try-with-resources does it in reverse order.

beats.text: Fetch the orders for customer 42. prepareStatement takes the SQL template. setLong binds 42. executeQuery hits MySQL and returns a ResultSet. The loop reads each order row. Here's the non-obvious part. When the try block ends, everything closes on its own.

items: Using executeQuery for an INSERT. It throws an error, so use executeUpdate instead.
Reading a column before the first next call. The cursor sits before row one.

questions.question: What are the main interfaces in the JDBC API?
questions.title: Core JDBC Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: The main JDBC interfaces include Driver, Connection, Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement, ResultSet, and DatabaseMetaData. DataSource is a javax.sql interface used to obtain connections. DriverManager is an important utility class, not an interface. JDBC code targets these contracts while a driver supplies most concrete implementations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the key JDBC interfaces and their responsibilities.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the Statement subtypes or thinking they're concrete classes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note these are interfaces implemented by the vendor driver — the source of JDBC portability.

sections.title: Core JDBC Types
sections.content:
Drivers also expose metadata, savepoints, arrays, blobs, and newer JDBC types through the same API family. Support for optional features can vary, so methods such as generated-key retrieval and scrollable result sets must be checked against the driver.

Use try-with-resources in reverse ownership order. Closing a Statement normally closes its current ResultSet, and closing a Connection closes its statements, but explicit scopes make ownership clear and return pooled connections promptly.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Connection represents a database session and transaction context.
Statement families execute SQL; PreparedStatement binds values; CallableStatement calls stored routines.
ResultSet is a cursor over tabular results.
DataSource is a connection factory; DriverManager is a class that locates drivers.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A typical application asks a DataSource for Connection, prepares SQL, binds values, executes, reads ResultSet, and closes each resource. SQLException is the checked exception family used for failures, but it is a class rather than an interface. Distinguishing contracts from utility classes prevents the inaccurate list 'DataSource, DriverManager, and Driver are all core interfaces'.

sections.title: JDBC Interfaces at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Connection|~DB session|creates statements|controls transactions|close when done
emerald|Statement family|~run SQL|Statement = static|PreparedStatement = params|CallableStatement = procs
amber|ResultSet|~read rows|cursor over results|next() + getXxx()|forward by default
violet|DataSource/Driver|~get connections|DataSource = pooled|DriverManager = direct|driver implements all

sections.title: Interfaces in one snippet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating them as classes**: they're interfaces implemented by the driver.
- **Confusing the Statement subtypes**: Statement (static), PreparedStatement (params), CallableStatement (procedures).
- **Forgetting `DataSource`**: it's the modern entry point, not `DriverManager`.
- **Assuming ResultSet is scrollable**: it's forward-only by default.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Since **JDBC 4.0**, drivers are **auto-loaded** via the Service Provider mechanism — just having the driver JAR on the classpath registers it, so `Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")` is **no longer needed**. You only call `Class.forName` for old drivers or non-standard setups.

questions.question: How does JDBC fit into a typical Spring Boot application architecture?
questions.title: JDBC in Spring Boot Architecture
questions.direct_answer: In a typical Spring Boot app, JDBC sits at the **bottom** of the data layer. Spring auto-configures a pooled **DataSource** (HikariCP) from `application.properties`; on top of it you use **Spring Data JPA / Hibernate** (or `JdbcTemplate`), which ultimately issue **JDBC** calls through that DataSource to the database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand JDBC is the foundation under Spring's data abstractions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking JPA/Hibernate bypass JDBC, or that you wire DataSource manually.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace the layers: Repository → JPA/Hibernate → DataSource (Hikari) → JDBC driver → DB.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **JDBC is the foundation** under Spring's data layer.
- **Spring Boot auto-configures** a pooled DataSource (HikariCP).
- **JPA/Hibernate and `JdbcTemplate`** issue JDBC calls underneath.
- **Layers**: Repository → Hibernate → DataSource → driver → DB.
- **You configure** the DataSource via `application.properties`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In a typical Spring Boot application, JDBC sits right at the bottom of the data access layer; Spring doesn't replace JDBC, it layers convenient abstractions on top of it. When you add a data starter and put your database URL, username, and password in application.properties, Spring Boot auto-configures a connection pool DataSource for you, and by default that's HikariCP. You almost never wire it up by hand. On top of that DataSource, your code works with a high-level abstraction. Most commonly that's a Spring Data JPA repository, where you just declare an interface method like findByCity and Hibernate generates the SQL. Hibernate, in turn, uses the DataSource to get a JDBC connection and runs the query through the JDBC driver. If you want something closer to raw SQL with less boilerplate, you can use JdbcTemplate, which is a thin Spring wrapper directly over JDBC. So the request flows down through layers: a controller calls a service, the service calls a repository, the repository goes through Hibernate or JPA, which goes through the DataSource pool, which hands out a JDBC connection, and the driver finally talks to the database. The key insight is that even when you're writing JPA repositories and never see a Connection object, JDBC is still doing the actual work underneath.

sections.title: A Query Through the Spring Boot Data Layer
sections.content:
Spring Boot first creates a `DataSource` from explicit application configuration and classpath conditions. In the usual JDBC starter, HikariCP provides the pool. Borrowing a `Connection` from that pool is different from opening a brand-new database socket for every repository call; closing the connection returns it to the pool.

`JdbcTemplate` works directly above JDBC. It obtains a connection, prepares and executes SQL, turns each `ResultSet` row into an application value, translates many `SQLException` values into Spring's data-access exception hierarchy, and releases resources. Application code still owns the SQL and row mapping.

JPA adds another layer. A Spring Data repository delegates to a JPA provider such as Hibernate, which maps entity operations to SQL. The provider still reaches the database through JDBC and the same `DataSource`. That means pool exhaustion, transaction boundaries, database locks, and slow SQL remain relevant even when no repository method contains JDBC code.

For a request such as `GET /orders/42`, the useful trace is controller → service → repository or template → transaction-bound connection → JDBC driver → database. The return path maps rows or entities back to the service and response. The abstraction changes who writes SQL and mapping code; it does not remove the database protocol beneath it.

sections.title: Spring Boot Data Layer
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  CTRL[Controller] --> SVC[Service]
  SVC --> REPO[Spring Data JPA Repository]
  REPO --> HIB[Hibernate / JPA provider]
  HIB --> DS[DataSource HikariCP pool]
  DS --> DRV[JDBC Driver]
  DRV --> DB[(Database)]
```

sections.title: Spring auto-configures the DataSource; JDBC runs underneath
Choose the highest layer that keeps the query clear
sections.content: Spring Data JPA removes routine repository code and is convenient for entity-oriented work. `JdbcTemplate` keeps SQL visible and gives direct control over query shape and row mapping. Raw JDBC is useful for learning and for narrow low-level integrations, but it carries the most resource and error-handling code. All three still depend on sound transactions, bounded connection pools, parameterized SQL, and database-aware tests.
